D:\\wt\\ckrules\\vlog\\ckrules\\voz\\b00.text: Rule number one, and nobody ever wrote it down. Hold that spoon still for a second, honey, and watch what I do with the water. Warm, not hot. 60 years in a church basement kitchen taught me that one little thing is the difference between rolls people fight over and rolls that come back to the pan with nothing left on them. Hello, honey, I'm Loretta. I'm 81 years old, and for 60 of those years, I cooked in the basement kitchen of our little church in Story County, Iowa. Funerals, weddings, Wednesday suppers, the men's pancake breakfast. If there was food on a long table, I was probably standing behind it with a spoon. My grandson Danny set this camera up on my kitchen table and said, Grandma, tell them the tricks before they're gone. You followed a recipe to the letter, and it still came out wrong. People write to me about it every week. The pie was runny.

The rolls were heavy as a brick, and every time the person says the same thing, but I did exactly what it said. Well honey, the recipe told you what to put in the bowl. It never told you the little things the ladies whispered while the coffee perked. Those are the things that make the dish. Today I'm giving you 12 of those rules. Every one of them is printed in my little cookbook, Loretta's Church Supper Cookbook. One recipe per page. I'll tell you who taught me each trick, why it works, and what goes wrong without it. Some will make you laugh. A couple will make you mad at yourself for never trying them. Get your apron on, let's go. The first rule came from a woman named Irene. Her dinner rolls came out of the church oven, 200 at a time, and half the rolls on the fellowship hall roof were hers. Everybody asked for the recipe, and she always said the same thing.

It's in the water, honey. Not the flour, not the butter, the water. Rule number one is Irene's potato water dinner rolls step by step, the way I'd tell it, standing at my stove. You need one medium russet potato, peeled and cubed, one packet of active dry yeast, one cup of milk, a third of a cup of sugar, a third of a cup of butter, and one egg, one and a half teaspoons of salt, about five cups of flour, makes 24 rolls. First, boil that potato in about two cups of water until soft, 15 to 20 minutes. Do not pour that water down the sink, save it. Mash the potato and measure out half a cup. Then cool half a cup of that potato water down to 110 degrees. That's warm, like a baby's bath, not hot. Hot water kills the yeast, and then your rolls never rise. Sprinkle the yeast and a pinch of sugar over that warm potato water. Now wait 10 minutes.

Go set the table. It should foam up like the head on a root beer. If it just sits there, honey, the yeast is dead and you need to start over with new yeast. Don't argue with it. Yeast is alive and it only works for you when it is comfortable. While the yeast wakes up, warm the milk with the butter and the sugar until the butter melts, then cool it to warm. In a big bowl, stir together the foamy yeast, the milk, the egg, the mashed potato and the salt. Add the flour one cup at a time until the dough pulls away from the side of the bowl. Trust the dough, not the measuring cup. Knead that dough eight full minutes until it feels smooth and a little tacky, like a ripe peach. Cover it and set it somewhere warm until it doubles, about one hour. Don't open the oven door to check on it. Warm and quiet is all it wants. Punch the dough down and cut it into 24 pieces.

Roll each into a smooth ball. Now, the part people skip. Set them touching in two buttered 9x13 pans. Let them rise another 45 minutes. When they touch, they push each other up and you get soft sides instead of hard crusts. Bake them at 375 degrees for 18 to 20 minutes until they are golden on top. Then brush them with butter while they are still hot. Eat one warm, that's allowed. Nobody in my family has ever once gotten a roll to the table cold and complained about it. So why does the potato water work? The potato gives the yeast a little starch to feed on and the water carries moisture into the dough. That keeps these rolls pillowy and soft for two full days on the counter. This recipe is on page 40 of my little cookbook with the trick, the common mistakes and the crowd amounts for a supper of 200.

The link to the cookbook is right under this video. Go on and make the rolls this week and take a few to somebody who needs them. That's what they were for. Rule number two comes from my mother and it's about the sweet potatoes at Thanksgiving. Mama never boiled a sweet potato in her life. She baked them whole in their skins on a foil -lined pan until a knife went in with a little push. The first time I boiled them, the syrup went thin as water and I heard about it from every woman in the kitchen. Boiled potatoes drink the water and then your syrup has nothing to hold on to. Baked potatoes are sweeter and hold their shape. Bake about four pounds of sweet potatoes, six of them, at 400 degrees for 40 to 45 minutes. Cool 15 minutes, slip off the skins and cut thick one -inch rounds. Now the syrup.

Melt half a cup of butter with a cup of packed brown sugar, a quarter cup of orange juice, a teaspoon of cinnamon, a quarter teaspoon of nutmeg, and half a teaspoon of salt. Simmer three minutes, then stir in a teaspoon of vanilla. Lay the rounds in a buttered pan, overlapping like shingles, and pour the syrup over. Bake at 375 for 30 to 35 minutes, spooning the syrup over the top every 10 minutes. That's basting, honey, don't skip it. Rule number three is for the sour cream raisin pie. It sounds strange if you are not from Iowa, and I won't argue with you about it, just make it once. The trick is one simple thing. Before you make the filling, cover your raisins with hot water and let them soak for 10 minutes, then drain them well. Dry raisins drink the filling, and then your pie is gummy with hard little pebbles in every bite.

Soaked raisins stay plump and juicy. 10 minutes in hot water. That's the whole secret, and it costs you nothing but a little patience. Rule number four is the lemon meringue pie, the queen of the church table. Tall golden peaks and sour enough to make your eyes water. Here is the rule. The meringue goes on a hot filling, never a cold one. Right after you pour the lemon filling into the baked crust, you spread the meringue over it while it is still hot, and you spread it all the way to the crust, sealing it all the way around. The heat from the filling cooks the meringue from underneath. When you seal it to the crust, it can't slide. If you put it on a cold filling, the sugar beads up and little syrup drops, and the meringue slides right off the lemon like a wet hat. Rule number five is for deviled eggs, the first plate empty at every potluck I ever worked.

Here is a trick nobody believes me about. You mash the cooked yolks and you season them first. Mustard, a tablespoon of dill pickle juice, a teaspoon of sugar, salt and pepper, until you have a stiff yellow paste. Then you stop, walk away for two minutes. Set a timer if you need to. A cooked yolk is dry and thirsty. It has to drink that seasoning before the mayonnaise goes in or the seasoning just sits on top. Then stir in half a cup of mayonnaise until it's smooth. The filling comes out silky and seasoned all the way through. Mix the mayo in first and you get lumps every time. Rule number six is for the three bean salad. It is better the day after you make it and nothing in it spoils sitting out in the sun. You open a can of green beans, a can of yellow wax beans and a can of red kidney beans and you drain them and you rinse the kidney beans well. Don't skip that rinse.

Otherwise, everything in the bowl turns pink. Warm the cider vinegar and the sugar in a little pan just until the sugar dissolves. Whisk in the oil, the salt, the pepper and the celery seed and pour it over the beans while it's still warm. Warm beans drink that dressing right in. Cold beans just sit in it like a puddle. Chill it overnight, stirring once or twice. Now honey, I want you to point your phone at the little square on the screen. That's the cookbook. It has all 50 recipes, one page each, and it's the same pages you're watching me read from right now. Take a look and come back. I'll wait. Rule number 7 is for the macaroni salad. Church Basement Macaroni Salad. Sweet and tangy and creamy. Here is the trick. You make the dressing extra and you save one third of it in the refrigerator. Do not toss all of it in at once. Macaroni is thirsty.

D:\\wt\\ckrules\\vlog\\ckrules\\voz\\b01.text: It drinks up the first batch of dressing overnight and by the next afternoon the salad is dry. So right before it goes on the table, you stir in that saved dressing. It makes the salad creamy all over again. Cook the pasta a minute past tender for a cold salad and drain it well. Rule number eight is for cheesy potatoes. Some people call them funeral potatoes and every family and morning in our town got a pan of them. They are comfort you can eat with a spoon. The trick is in the potatoes themselves. You take the thawed hash browns and you wring them dry. Put them in a clean dish towel and squeeze with both hands until nothing else comes out. That water is what turns a pan of cheesy potatoes into potato soup. Ring them and the sauce stays thick and the potatoes stay tender.

Make the topping with crushed corn flakes tossed in the rest of the melted butter and bake it uncovered at 350 for 50 to 55 minutes. Covered, the topping goes soggy. Uncovered, it crunches. Rule number nine is for the potato puff hot dish, Iowa's favorite Friday supper. You brown the ground beef and the onion, season it with salt, pepper, and a little Worcestershire, and stir in two soups, the milk and the green beans. Spread it in the pan, sprinkle the cheese on top, and then comes the part that matters. You take the potato puffs, still frozen, and you line them up on top in neat rows, standing close together like little soldiers. Do not thaw those potato puffs. Frozen ones crisp up on top while the bottom drinks up the gravy underneath. Thawed ones go soft and soggy.

Bake it uncovered at 375 for 40 to 45 minutes until the potatoes are deep golden and taste the sauce before you add salt because both soups already have salt in them. Rule number 10 is for the church basement hamburger hot dish. This one fed 200 plates. I cooked the big pans for funerals and it never let me down. Here is the trick. You boil the noodles two minutes less than the package says. Two minutes short. They are going to finish cooking inside the sauce and when they soak up that sauce instead of water they taste like supper and not like paste. When the hot dish comes out of the oven let it sit 10 minutes before you scoop. I have watched people dig into a hot pan like they were digging for buried treasure and it runs all over the plate. 10 minutes and it holds together on the spoon. Rule 11 is the brown sugar ham.

Church Supper Ham, the Easter Ham. Here is the trick and it's a big one. The glaze goes on in the last 20 to 30 minutes, never at the start. You put that ham in the roasting pan cut side down, pour a cup of apple juice in the bottom, and cover it tightly with foil. Bake it at 275, about 15 minutes for every pound. Sugar cannot sit in a hot oven for two hours without turning black, and that's why the people who brush it on at the beginning end up with bitter ham. So simmer the brown sugar, honey, mustard, cider vinegar, and a pinch of cloves for two minutes. When the center reads about 120 degrees, take off the foil, raise the oven to 400, and brush on half the glaze. Then the rest, 10 minutes later. Now listen to me for one minute about temperature because it matters more than any glaze.

A fully cooked ham is reheated to 140 degrees. Hot food stays at 140 or above on the table and cold food at 40 or below. Nothing sits out more than two hours and that is one hour on a hot summer day. Chicken and turkey go to 165. Ground beef and ham balls go to 160. Pork chops go to 145. Then rest three minutes. That's not a suggestion. It's the rule. Rule number 12 is the one I saved for last because it is the one people ask me about most. It's Bernice's slow cooker pot roast. Bernice was my friend in that basement kitchen for 30 years. She was a big laughing woman with flour on her glasses and she put a cup of strong black coffee in her pot roast. Nobody believed her. Nobody believes me either until they taste the gravy. Here is how she did it.

Pat a three to four pound chuck roast dry and salt and pepper every side. Brown it hard in hot oil, four minutes a side, until it's dark brown. Gray meat makes flat gravy and no amount of coffee will fix that. Put the onions in the bottom of the slow cooker, then the carrots, the potatoes and the garlic. The meat goes on top of the vegetables, not underneath. Pour a cup of strong black coffee and a cup of beef broth into that hot skillet, scrape up the brown bits, add a tablespoon of Worcestershire and pour it over the roast. Tuck in two bay leaves, cook on low for eight hours and don't you dare lift the lid. When a fork twists the meat apart, lift it out, skim the fat and stir in three tablespoons of mixed with three of cold water. Boil one minute and you have gravy. The coffee makes it deep and dark and you will never once taste coffee. That's the secret.

Bernice was my friend in that basement kitchen for 30 years. She was a big laughing woman with flour on her glasses. And she used to say, honey, the good cooks keep one secret and they only tell you when you ask the right way. Her roast is on my table every Sunday. Here are the 12 quick so you can remember them. One, warm the potato water to 110. Two, bake sweet potatoes in their skins. Three, soak the raisins 10 minutes. Four, the meringue goes on a hot filling. Five, season the yolks and wait two minutes. Six, pour the bean dressing on warm. Seven, save a third of the macaroni dressing. Eight, wring the potatoes dry. Nine, frozen potato puffs go on top. 10, let the hot dish rest. 11, glaze the ham at the end. And 12, vegetables on the bottom, meat on top and a cup of coffee.

Every one of those tricks is printed on a page of my cookbook with the recipe, the amounts for a crowd and the amounts for one or two. The link to Loretta's Church Supper Cookbook is right under this video and page 40 has the rules. Print the one page you're cooking and stand it against the flower canister. Now I want you to tell me something in the comments, honey. Which of these 12 rules did your grandmother teach you or which one did you never know? Write it down. I read every single one and I answer when I can. Next week I'm going to show you the smothered pork chops our church served at every funeral dinner. Fork tender, never tough and the trick is a salt bath before the pan. Some of you already asked me about it on the last video and I haven't forgotten.

And if you want to see another one of my old church recipes, there is a video on this channel called 12 Things Church Ladies Never Threw Away. It's about the kitchen drawers and the tins we kept and some of them will surprise you. Go on now, cook something, warm the water, wait for the yeast and take a plate to somebody who needs it. That is what the recipes were for in the first place. God bless you honey and I will see you in the church basement.
